subject: feminism
title: First Wave (c. 1848–1920): the fight over whether women counted as political persons
dek: From Seneca Falls to the Nineteenth Amendment, women in the United States and Britain organized for the vote and for legal standing. The movement split over race, tactics, and who was included when organizers said “we.”

thumb.alt: Carte-de-visite of Sojourner Truth, standing with a cane, spectacles, and a white cap, 1864.

hero.alt: Inez Milholland in a white cape on a white horse at the Woman Suffrage Procession, Washington, D.C., 3 March 1913. A crowd lines the street; the print is captioned Suffrage parade 3/3/13.
hero.caption: Inez Milholland riding at the head of the Woman Suffrage Procession in Washington, D.C., on 3 March 1913, the day before Woodrow Wilson’s inauguration. Organizers put her there so the parade would have a clear public image. The rest of this lesson is about who was allowed to march in that line, and who was asked to wait.

honesty: “First wave” is a later Anglo-American classroom name. The people in this lesson did not call themselves that. The label is useful because it groups several decades of public campaigns over whether women counted as political persons. It is incomplete as a history, because those campaigns were not only Anglo-American, and because they did not include every woman they claimed to speak for. What follows uses the usual dates, then looks at the same years in China.

timeline.label: Seneca Falls
timeline.detail: A two-day convention in Seneca Falls, New York, issued the Declaration of Sentiments. The vote was one demand among many legal and social grievances.

timeline.label: Akron
timeline.detail: Sojourner Truth spoke at a women’s rights meeting in Akron, Ohio. The famous refrain “Ain’t I a woman?” comes from a later rewrite of that speech.

timeline.label: The split
timeline.detail: The Fifteenth Amendment barred denying the vote because of race, not sex. Stanton and Anthony opposed ratifying it without women; Stone and Douglass would not block Black men’s suffrage in order to wait.

timeline.label: Anqing
timeline.detail: Qiu Jin was executed after an uprising in Anqing. She was working in the same decade as British militant suffragettes, under a different government.

timeline.label: Procession / Derby
timeline.detail: On 3 March, Alice Paul and Lucy Burns organized a suffrage procession in Washington, D.C. In June, Emily Wilding Davison died after stepping onto the course at the Epsom Derby.

timeline.label: Nineteenth Amendment
timeline.detail: The United States barred denying the vote because of sex. Poll taxes, literacy tests, and violence still blocked many Black women in the South.

watch.title: Time to Remember — Time of the Suffragettes (1911–1913)
watch.note: British Pathé compilation of British suffragette newsreel, 1911–1913. This is not film of the 1913 Washington procession.

watch.title: The Derby — 1912 & 1913
watch.note: British Pathé racing newsreel. It includes the 1913 Epsom Derby, when Emily Wilding Davison stepped onto the course. Again: Britain, not Pennsylvania Avenue.

glossary.explain: English common-law doctrine that a married woman’s legal identity was “covered” by her husband’s. Property, contracts, and wages were his unless a statute carved out an exception.

A nineteenth-century middle-class rule: men belonged in public and economic life, and women belonged in the home as moral guardians. It was a class rule as much as a sex rule. Women who earned wages, and enslaved women, were never offered that protected private role.

Village in western New York. On 19–20 July 1848 a convention there issued the Declaration of Sentiments. Later writers used “Seneca Falls” as shorthand for the start of organized U.S. women’s rights. It is a useful date, not the only origin.
The 1848 Seneca Falls text, modeled on the Declaration of Independence. It listed grievances including the vote. The vote was not the only demand, and not everyone in the room wanted it named first.
Ratified 1870. It barred denying the vote “on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude.” It did not mention sex. The omission split the U.S. women’s-rights coalition.
Women’s Social and Political Union, founded 1903 by Emmeline Pankhurst. The militant wing of British suffrage: window-breaking, hunger strikes, and, in reply, force-feeding.
The system of legal racial segregation and disenfranchisement in the U.S. South after Reconstruction — poll taxes, literacy tests, violence. The Nineteenth Amendment did not repeal it.
Chinese Women’s Journal, edited by Qiu Jin in Shanghai in 1907. Two issues appeared. It argued for women’s education and against bound feet in the same breath as anti-Qing politics.
A small albumen photograph mounted on card, cheap to reproduce, sold and collected in the 1860s. Sojourner Truth sold hers with a printed caption and a copyright in her own name.

Frances Dana Gage. In 1863 she published a version of Sojourner Truth’s 1851 Akron speech that includes the refrain “Ain’t I a woman?” Contemporary 1851 newspaper accounts do not use the refrain that way.
Ratified 1920. It says the right to vote shall not be denied on account of sex. It did not touch poll taxes, literacy tests, or the violence that still blocked many Black women in the South.

In British prisons, hunger-striking suffragettes were restrained and fed through a tube. The Liberal government presented it as medical care. Militants presented it as assault. Both descriptions circulated in the press.

A later name for organized U.S. feminism in the 1920s–1950s. After the vote arrived, the suffrage coalition thinned and public campaigning quieted. The word describes one organized current going quiet. It does not mean the underlying questions ended.

American suffrage organizer. She trained with British militants, then with Lucy Burns planned the 3 March 1913 Woman Suffrage Procession in Washington. She later led the National Woman’s Party and wrote an Equal Rights Amendment.

State statutes, beginning in the 1840s, that let a married woman keep some property in her own name. New York’s 1848 act is the usual example. The laws were limited and uneven. They did not end coverture.

Founded in 1869 by Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony after the split over the Fifteenth Amendment. It opposed ratifying the amendment without women and worked for a federal suffrage amendment.
Founded in 1869 by Lucy Stone and others who would not block Black men’s suffrage in order to wait for women. It favored a state-by-state strategy. It merged with the NWSA in 1890.

The 1890 merger of the National Woman Suffrage Association and the American Woman Suffrage Association. The main constitutional-suffrage organization in the United States until the Nineteenth Amendment.

aliases: Prisoners Temporary Discharge for Ill Health Act
glossary.explain: British 1913 statute that released hunger-striking suffragettes when they were too weak to feed, then rearrested them when they recovered. The nickname compared the government to a cat playing with a mouse.
Anti-Qing revolutionary. His 1907 uprising in Anqing failed. Qiu Jin, who had been working with the same network, was arrested and executed afterward.

fun_fact.title: She copyrighted her own photograph
fun_fact.text: In 1864 Sojourner Truth registered the copyright on her own cartes-de-visite in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan. That was unusual: the photographer usually claimed the image. The cards were printed with her own sentence, “I sell the shadow to support the substance.” She sold them at lectures because lectures did not pay enough. The portrait in this lesson is one of those cards. The “shadow” here is her word for the photograph, not a later flourish.

sections.title: Married women had no separate legal self, and abolition trained the organizers

blocks.text: Under English common law, a married woman’s legal identity was absorbed into her husband’s. The doctrine is called coverture. Her property, her contracts, and her wages belonged to him unless a statute carved out an exception. An unmarried woman had more legal room. Marriage closed it. In the United States, states began to pass Married Women’s Property Acts in the 1840s — New York’s 1848 statute is the usual example — but those laws were limited, uneven, and did not make a wife a full legal person.

Industrial work had already left the house. What remained, for middle-class white women, was a public story about respectability: the home as a moral refuge, the woman as domestic, delicate, and good. Historians call this “separate spheres.” It was a rule of class as much as of sex. Enslaved women, and women who worked for wages, were never offered that protected private role. They were already in public as labor, as property, or as exceptions the ideology did not have to explain.

Abolition was the training ground for many United States feminists. In anti-slavery societies they learned to petition legislatures, lecture to mixed audiences, edit newspapers, and run a meeting. Those skills transferred to women’s rights. The alliance later cracked, after the Civil War, when the question became which emancipation would be allowed to go first: Black men’s suffrage, or women’s.

sections.title: Seneca Falls, the Fifteenth Amendment split, and the 1913 parade

blocks.text: On 19–20 July 1848, at Seneca Falls, New York, a convention issued a Declaration of Sentiments modeled on the Declaration of Independence. Elizabeth Cady Stanton was the principal author; Lucretia Mott was among the organizers. The vote was one grievance among others — property, divorce, education, and public speech. Not everyone in the room wanted the vote named first. The document still did something new in American public life: it treated women as people who could claim the same political rights the United States had already claimed for men.

blocks.alt: Printed souvenir card titled Our Roll of Honor, listing women who signed the 1848 Declaration of Sentiments.
blocks.caption: A 1908 souvenir card titled “Our Roll of Honor,” printed sixty years after Seneca Falls, listing the women who signed the 1848 Declaration of Sentiments. Lucretia Mott and Elizabeth Cady Stanton head the first column. This is a commemorative card, not the 1848 manuscript.

blocks.text: In 1851 Sojourner Truth spoke at a women’s rights meeting in Akron, Ohio. The famous refrain “Ain’t I a woman?” comes from Frances Dana Gage’s 1863 rewrite of that speech. Contemporary 1851 newspaper accounts do not use the refrain that way. The later version is the one that traveled in print. The historical point does not depend on the catchphrase. A feminism built on white middle-class delicacy treated enslaved women and working women as exceptions — people whose bodies had already been asked to do too much to count as the “woman” the movement was picturing.

After the Civil War the coalition split over the Fifteenth Amendment, ratified in 1870, which barred denying the vote “on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude.” It did not mention sex. In 1869 Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony founded the National Woman Suffrage Association and opposed ratifying the amendment without women. Lucy Stone and others founded the American Woman Suffrage Association and would not block Black men’s suffrage in order to wait. Frederick Douglass, who had supported women’s rights at Seneca Falls, took Stone’s side on sequence. The argument was about order, and about who was being asked to stand aside. The two organizations did not merge into the National American Woman Suffrage Association until 1890.

In Britain the movement divided by method. Constitutional suffragists collected signatures and lobbied Parliament. The militant Women’s Social and Political Union, founded in 1903 by Emmeline Pankhurst, broke windows, disrupted meetings, and, in prison, went on hunger strike. The Liberal government answered with force-feeding, then with the 1913 Prisoners (Temporary Discharge for Ill-Health) Act — the “Cat and Mouse Act” — which released weakened prisoners and rearrested them when they recovered. In June 1913 Emily Wilding Davison died after stepping onto the course at the Epsom Derby in front of the king’s horse.

blocks.alt: Formal seated portrait of Emmeline Pankhurst, 1913.
blocks.caption: Emmeline Pankhurst in 1913, the year Emily Wilding Davison died at Epsom and the Women’s Social and Political Union’s militancy was impossible to ignore. Constitutional suffragists were still collecting signatures. Pankhurst’s organization was collecting prison sentences.

blocks.text: On 3 March 1913, the day before Wilson’s inauguration, Alice Paul and Lucy Burns organized the Woman Suffrage Procession in Washington, D.C. Inez Milholland rode in white on a white horse at the head of the line. Black women were told to march in a rear contingent. Ida B. Wells refused. She waited until the Illinois delegation passed, then stepped into that line and marched with her state.

blocks.alt: A dense crowd lining Pennsylvania Avenue to watch the 1913 woman suffrage procession in Washington, D.C.
blocks.caption: The crowd on Pennsylvania Avenue, 3 March 1913. Men climbed poles and wagons to see. Alice Paul timed the procession for the eve of Woodrow Wilson’s inauguration so it could not be missed. Being unmissable was not the same as being welcomed: spectators repeatedly stepped into the street and broke the line of march.

blocks.alt: Color official program cover for the Woman Suffrage Procession, Washington, D.C., 3 March 1913, showing a woman on horseback before the Capitol.
blocks.caption: The official program for the same day. The horse, the banner, and the Capitol show who the procession wanted to look like. Ida B. Wells’s decision to leave the “rear contingent” and walk with the Illinois delegation is the part the program does not print.

blocks.text: The Nineteenth Amendment was ratified in 1920. It says the right to vote shall not be denied on account of sex. It did not repeal Jim Crow. Many Black women in the South were still blocked by poll taxes, literacy tests, and violence. The amendment changed the federal text. The local machinery that decided who could actually cast a ballot did not change with it.

The same years, in a different country: Qiu Jin 秋瑾 (1875–1907). She unbound her feet, left an arranged marriage, studied in Japan from 1904, and in 1907 edited 中國女報 (the Chinese Women’s Journal) in Shanghai. The journal argued for women’s education and against bound feet in the same pages as anti-Qing politics. After Xu Xilin’s uprising in Anqing failed, she was arrested and executed. Her public life does not sit on a line from Seneca Falls to 1920. It belongs in the same decades anyway: a woman deciding she would count in public, under a different state, and paying for it with her life.

sections.title: Four people the usual story has to include

people.name: Sojourner Truth
people.alt: 1864 carte-de-visite of Sojourner Truth standing with a cane. Printed caption: I sell the shadow to support the substance.
people.caption: Carte-de-visite, 1864, printed with her own line: “I sell the shadow to support the substance.”
people.text: Born enslaved in New York. She sold cartes-de-visite captioned “I sell the shadow to support the substance.” The card was a living: lectures did not pay enough, and she needed the sales. It was also a legal claim. She copyrighted the image in her own name, which was unusual for a sitter, and still more unusual for a woman who had been treated as property.

people.name: Ida B. Wells
people.alt: Studio portrait of Ida B. Wells-Barnett by Mary Garrity, about 1893.
people.caption: Ida B. Wells-Barnett, photographed by Mary Garrity around 1893.
people.text: Anti-lynching journalist; Southern Horrors appeared in 1892. She treated suffrage and racial terror as one fight, which is why a segregated parade order in 1913 was not a small slight. She refused the rear contingent and walked into the Illinois line as it passed.

people.name: Inez Milholland
people.alt: Inez Milholland on a white horse in the 1913 suffrage procession, Washington, D.C.
people.caption: Milholland on Pennsylvania Avenue, 3 March 1913: white cape, white horse, a planned public image.
people.text: Lawyer, and the image the 1913 procession needed at its head. She died in 1916 on a western suffrage tour, at thirty. The photograph of her on the white horse outlived the campaign she was riding for.

people.name: Qiu Jin 秋瑾
people.alt: Portrait of Qiu Jin, photographed in the last years of the Qing dynasty, between 1900 and 1907.
people.caption: Qiu Jin, photographed between 1900 and 1907, in the last years of the Qing dynasty.
people.text: Unbound feet, study in Japan, editor of 中國女報, executed after the 1907 Anqing uprising. If the phrase “first wave” cannot hold her, the phrase is too narrow. Her life is not the problem.

sections.title: “I sell the shadow to support the substance”

blocks.alt: Sojourner Truth’s 1864 carte-de-visite, with the printed line I sell the shadow to support the substance under her portrait.
blocks.caption: Sojourner Truth, 1864. She sold the card because lectures did not pay enough. She also put her own copyright on it.

blocks.text: Truth sold her image because lectures did not pay enough. On the card, the “shadow” is the photograph — a thing that can be reproduced, captioned, and passed from hand to hand. The “substance” is the work, and the body that had been treated as property. She put the sentence on the card in English, under her own name, and made the sale part of the argument: I will be paid for the copy of me that you can hold.

Keep the card in mind when a movement talks about “women” as if the category were already settled. Someone is always deciding which body is the subject of the campaign, and which body is only used to illustrate it.

sections.title: After 1920 the coalition thinned, and a later generation named a second wave

blocks.text: In the United States the 1920s through the 1950s are often called the “doldrums”: the vote arrived, and the suffrage coalition thinned. The word is a later summary, not a name people used at the time. It describes a particular organized feminism going quiet. It does not mean the questions ended, and it does not mean every woman had been in that coalition.

What later writers called the second wave — the 1960s and 1970s — turned to the workplace, to sexuality, and to housework. “The personal is political” became a slogan for that turn. The who-counts problem returned in public, including in the Combahee River Collective statement of 1977, which refused to treat race, sex, and class as separate queues.

The wave metaphor itself is a later teaching device. It offers a tidy sequence: first the vote, then the rest. It hides the people who were never in that sequence — and the fights that did not wait for the next numbered period.
When a movement says “we,” who is being asked to wait?
